## Solution

We seek $\inf S$ where $S = \{\alpha > 0 : X_n^{(\alpha)} \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} 0\}$.

**Key observation.** Since $X_n^{(\alpha)} \in \{0,1\}$, we have $X_n^{(\alpha)} \to 0$ a.s. if and only if $X_n^{(\alpha)} = 1$ only finitely often, i.e.,
$$P\!\left(X_n^{(\alpha)} = 1 \text{ i.o.}\right) = 0.$$

**Applying Borel–Cantelli.** The events $\{X_n^{(\alpha)} = 1\}$ are independent (since the $X_n^{(\alpha)}$ are independent). Set $A_n = \{X_n^{(\alpha)} = 1\}$ with $P(A_n) = \frac{1}{n^{2\alpha}}$.

- **First Borel–Cantelli lemma** (no independence needed): If $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} P(A_n) < \infty$, then $P(A_n \text{ i.o.}) = 0$.
- **Second Borel–Cantelli lemma** (requires independence): If $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} P(A_n) = \infty$, then $P(A_n \text{ i.o.}) = 1$.

The series in question is the $p$-series
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^{2\alpha}},$$
which converges if and only if $2\alpha > 1$, i.e., $\alpha > \tfrac{1}{2}$.

**Case 1: $\alpha > \tfrac{1}{2}$.** The series converges, so by the first Borel–Cantelli lemma, $P(X_n^{(\alpha)} = 1 \text{ i.o.}) = 0$, hence $X_n^{(\alpha)} \to 0$ a.s. Thus $\alpha \in S$.

**Case 2: $0 < \alpha \leq \tfrac{1}{2}$.** The series diverges, and by independence the second Borel–Cantelli lemma gives $P(X_n^{(\alpha)} = 1 \text{ i.o.}) = 1$, hence $X_n^{(\alpha)} \not\to 0$ a.s. Thus $\alpha \notin S$.

**Conclusion.** We have shown
$$S = \left(\tfrac{1}{2},\, \infty\right),$$
and therefore
$$\inf S = \boxed{\dfrac{1}{2}}.$$

So $X_n^{(\alpha)} \to 0$ a.s. iff $\sum \frac{1}{n^{2\alpha}} < \infty$ iff $\alpha > 1/2$.

For $0 < \alpha \leq 1/2$, $\sum 1/n^{2\alpha} = \infty$, by second Borel-Cantelli (independence holds), $P(X_n = 1 \text{ i.o.}) = 1$, so $X_n \not\to 0$ a.s. So $\alpha \notin S$.
